pos: n. (king of the Amalekites spared by Saul and hewn in pieces by Samuel; the sparing cost Saul his throne)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Agag, of uncertain derivation; possibly a dynastic title of Amalekite kings rather than a personal name, since Balaam speaks of Agag generations earlier. Haman is later called the Agagite.
biblical_def: Agag is the king of Amalek in the reign of Saul, and his story is the hinge on which Saul's kingdom turns. Amalek had ambushed Israel's stragglers coming out of Egypt, and God had sworn perpetual war against them. Saul was given a plain command and executed it partially: “he took Agag the king of the Amalekites alive, and utterly destroyed all the people with the edge of the sword” (1Sa 15:8), and then “Saul and the people spared Agag, and the best of the sheep, and of the oxen… and would not utterly destroy them” (1Sa 15:9). He kept the king as a trophy and the livestock as spoil, and offered the pious excuse that the animals were for sacrifice. Samuel's answer is one of the great sentences of the Old Testament: to obey is better than sacrifice, and rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft. Then the prophet finished what the king would not: “Bring ye hither to me Agag the king of the Amalekites. And Agag came unto him delicately. And Agag said, Surely the bitterness of death is past” (1Sa 15:32) — and Samuel hewed him in pieces before the LORD in Gilgal (1Sa 15:33). Centuries later Haman the Agagite would try to destroy the Jews of Persia, which is what unfinished obedience tends to produce.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Agag; in sacred history he is a king of the Amalekites, spared by Saul contrary to the command of God, and slain by Samuel.
webster_full: AGAG, n. A king of the Amalekites, taken alive by Saul.
The name appears also in the prophecy of Balaam, and may have been a common title of their kings.
Saul spared him, and the best of the spoil, contrary to the express command of the LORD.
For this disobedience the kingdom was rent from Saul.
Samuel hewed Agag in pieces before the LORD in Gilgal.
scriptures: And he took Agag the king of the Amalekites alive, and utterly destroyed all the people with the edge of the sword.

But Saul and the people spared Agag, and the best of the sheep, and of the oxen, and of the fatlings, and the lambs, and all that was good, and would not utterly destroy them: but every thing that was vile and refuse, that they destroyed utterly.
Then said Samuel, Bring ye hither to me Agag the king of the Amalekites. And Agag came unto him delicately. And Agag said, Surely the bitterness of death is past.
And Samuel said, As thy sword hath made women childless, so shall thy mother be childless among women. And Samuel hewed Agag in pieces before the LORD in Gilgal.
corruption_summary: The command against Amalek is cited as proof that the God of the Old Testament is cruel, and Saul's partial obedience is treated as mercy rather than as the calculated self-will Samuel names it.
corruption_paragraphs: The judgment on Amalek is a standing exhibit in the modern case against the God of Israel, and the case is usually made without the facts. Amalek attacked the weakest of a defenceless people newly out of slavery, and God swore war against them “from generation to generation” (Exo 17:16) — a sentence pronounced by the Judge of all the earth and delayed some four hundred years, which is not haste. Scripture presents such judgments as judicial acts against nations whose iniquity was full, executed by God's own express command through His covenant nation, and never as a warrant for any later people to imitate. The church's weapons are not carnal (2Co 10:4). Those who find the doctrine severe should notice that the same God delayed the sentence four centuries, and that He held His hand over Nineveh when it repented.

The second corruption is closer to the pulpit: making Saul sympathetic. He kept the best animals and the royal captive, and explained that the beasts were for sacrifice — religious language over an act of self-will, with the blame placed on “the people”. Samuel refused all of it: “to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams. For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry” (1Sa 15:22-23). Partial obedience is disobedience with better public relations. Saul lost a kingdom over livestock he intended to worship God with, and the lesson stands over every ministry that keeps back a portion of the command and calls the remainder devotion.

usage: “Saul and the people spared Agag” — partial obedience, and a kingdom lost.
“Surely the bitterness of death is past” — the last words of a man who had misread his reprieve.
“To obey is better than sacrifice” — the whole doctrine in seven words.

pos: n. (the father of a race of giants in the hill country about Hebron, whose sons made ten of the twelve spies despair)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Anaq, connected with a word for a neck-chain or collar — long-necked, and so tall. His descendants are the Anakim, the sons of Anak.
biblical_def: Anak is the ancestor of the tall men who held the hill country around Hebron when the twelve spies went up. The report names them: “they ascended by the south, and came unto Hebron; where Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the children of Anak, were” (Num 13:22). Ten of the spies made the sight of them the argument against faith — the people be strong, the cities walled and very great, “and moreover we saw the children of Anak there” (Num 13:28) — and then went further: “there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight” (Num 13:33). That last sentence is the anatomy of unbelief. They measured themselves against the giants, decided what they looked like in another man's eyes, and never once put God into the comparison. Caleb did the arithmetic differently and never forgot it; forty-five years later, an old man, he asked for that very hill: give me this mountain, for the Anakims are there, “if so be the LORD will be with me, then I shall be able to drive them out” (Jos 14:12). And he did: “Caleb drove thence the three sons of Anak” (Jos 15:14) — the same three, named again, taken by the one man who had believed the LORD when the giants were only a rumour.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Anak; in sacred history he is the father of the Anakim, a race of giants dwelling about Hebron in the land of Canaan.
webster_full: ANAK, n. The father of the Anakim, a race of tall men in the south of Canaan.
His sons Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai dwelt at Hebron, called also Kirjath-arba.
The spies sent by Moses reported that they saw the children of Anak there.
The name is thought to signify long-necked, and so of great stature.
Caleb drove out the three sons of Anak when Hebron was given him for an inheritance.
scriptures: And they ascended by the south, and came unto Hebron; where Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the children of Anak, were. (Now Hebron was built seven years before Zoan in Egypt.)
Nevertheless the people be strong that dwell in the land, and the cities are walled, and very great: and moreover we saw the children of Anak there.
And there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.
And Caleb drove thence the three sons of Anak, Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai, the children of Anak.
corruption_summary: The Anakim are either dissolved into folklore or inflated into a mythology of fallen-angel hybrids; and the spies' unbelief is softened into understandable caution rather than named as the sin that killed a generation.
corruption_paragraphs: Two speculative excesses attend this text. The first treats the giants as legend, a folk memory dressed up to explain ruined walls. The second builds an elaborate mythology on the word rendered giants, linking the Anakim to the Nephilim of Genesis 6 and constructing a system of angelic-human hybrids surviving the flood. The dictionary keeps to what is written. Moses reports tall, formidable men in the hill country of Canaan; Deuteronomy compares their stature to the Emims and the Zamzummims; and the point of the passage is not their genetics but Israel's faith. Where Scripture is silent, speculation should be silent too — and a doctrine built on the fringes of Genesis 6 has left the ground of the plain word.

The second corruption is a pastoral one. The ten spies gave a report that was factually accurate in nearly every particular; their sin was not bad data but a comparison with God left out of it. Hebrews names the failure precisely: “they could not enter in because of unbelief” (Heb 3:19) — not because of the giants. Modern Christians are urged to be realistic about obstacles and are seldom warned that realism which never reaches as far as the promises of God is the very thing that killed a generation in the wilderness. Caleb saw the same walls and the same men. He simply added the LORD to the sum, and lived to take the mountain.

“We were in our own sight as grasshoppers” — unbelief measuring itself against the wrong thing.
“Caleb drove thence the three sons of Anak” — forty-five years later, the same three, by name.

pos: n. (one of the two kings of Midian pursued and slain by Gideon; his name means sacrifice)
etymology: From Hebrew Zebach, a sacrifice or slaughtered victim — a name whose sense was answered in the manner of his death. Scripture almost always pairs him with Zalmunna.
biblical_def: Zebah is named eleven times in Judges and never once alone. He and Zalmunna are the two surviving kings of Midian after the rout of the three hundred, and Gideon's pursuit of them across the Jordan is one of the grimmest passages in the book. Faint and still chasing, he asked bread of the men of Succoth and was mocked: are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in thine hand, that we should give bread unto thy men (Jdg 8:15)? He took the kings anyway — “when Zebah and Zalmunna fled, he pursued after them, and took the two kings of Midian” (Jdg 8:12) — came back and taught the men of Succoth with thorns and briers. Then came the question that explains the whole chase: “What manner of men were they whom ye slew at Tabor? And they answered, As thou art, so were they; each one resembled the children of a king” (Jdg 8:18). They had killed Gideon's brothers. This was blood vengeance as well as holy war. He ordered his firstborn son to kill them; the boy was afraid; and the kings themselves asked for a soldier's death: “Rise thou, and fall upon us: for as the man is, so is his strength. And Gideon arose, and slew Zebah and Zalmunna” (Jdg 8:21). Asaph keeps them as a byword: make all their princes as Zebah, and as Zalmunna (Psa 83:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Zebah; in sacred history he is one of the two kings of Midian taken and slain by Gideon beyond Jordan.
webster_full: ZEBAH, n. One of the two kings of Midian in the days of Gideon.
He is always named with Zalmunna, his fellow king.
They fled beyond Jordan with fifteen thousand men, and were pursued and taken at Karkor.
They had slain the brethren of Gideon at Tabor, and he required their blood.
The psalmist makes them a byword for the princes of the enemies of God's people.
scriptures: Jdg 8:5
And he said unto the men of Succoth, Give, I pray you, loaves of bread unto the people that follow me; for they be faint, and I am pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna, kings of Midian.
Jdg 8:12
And when Zebah and Zalmunna fled, he pursued after them, and took the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and discomfited all the host.
Jdg 8:18
Then said he unto Zebah and Zalmunna, What manner of men were they whom ye slew at Tabor? And they answered, As thou art, so were they; each one resembled the children of a king.
Jdg 8:21

Then Zebah and Zalmunna said, Rise thou, and fall upon us: for as the man is, so is his strength. And Gideon arose, and slew Zebah and Zalmunna, and took away the ornaments that were on their camels' necks.
corruption_summary: Gideon is flattened into a straightforward hero, when Judges deliberately shows the same man growing harsher through the chapter and ending in an ephod that became a snare to all Israel.
corruption_paragraphs: The children's-story Gideon — fleece, trumpets, three hundred men — stops before Judges 8, and Judges 8 is where the author is going. The man who began by asking for signs ends by threshing the elders of his own countrymen with thorns, tearing down a tower and killing its people, executing kings for family blood, and taking the golden earrings of the spoil to make an ephod “which thing became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house” (Jdg 8:27). The book is not endorsing this trajectory; it is recording it, in a volume whose refrain is that every man did that which was right in his own eyes. Scripture's heroes are given to us with their sins attached, which is one of the strongest evidences that it is not propaganda.

The second thing to name is the modern discomfort with blood vengeance, which usually produces either a squeamish silence or an attack on the text. Judges reports a world in which the avenger of blood was a recognized office, later regulated by the law of Moses with cities of refuge to restrain it. Scripture's trajectory is toward the removal of private vengeance altogether: “Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord” (Rom 12:19). Justice is not abolished; it is transferred to the magistrate and finally to God, who will not let one drop of innocent blood go unanswered.

“Each one resembled the children of a king” — the answer that named the debt.
“All their princes as Zebah, and as Zalmunna” — a psalm keeps them as a byword.

pos: n. (the second of the two kings of Midian taken and slain by Gideon beyond Jordan)
etymology: From Hebrew Tsalmunna', commonly explained as “shade withheld” or “protection denied” — from tsel, shadow or shelter, with a negative. Whatever the derivation, no shelter was found for him.
biblical_def: Zalmunna is the fellow king of Zebah, and the two are inseparable in the record. When the three hundred broke the Midianite host by night with pitchers and trumpets, these two escaped eastward with fifteen thousand men, and Gideon crossed Jordan after them — “I am pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna, kings of Midian” (Jdg 8:5) — on a march so hard that his men were fainting and two towns refused them bread. He took them at Karkor, came back by the way of the towns that had mocked him, and set the captive kings before the men of Succoth: “Behold Zebah and Zalmunna, with whom ye did upbraid me” (Jdg 8:15). Before the execution he asked one question and received one answer, and both are worth weighing. What manner of men were they whom ye slew at Tabor? — “As thou art, so were they; each one resembled the children of a king” (Jdg 8:18). The kings knew exactly whose brothers they had killed. Gideon's son Jether was ordered to strike and could not, being young and afraid; and the two men, contemptuous of the boy's hesitation, invited the father to do it himself, which he did (Jdg 8:21). Asaph prays that the enemies of God's people may go the same way (Psa 83:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Zalmunna; in sacred history he is the second of the two Midianite kings whom Gideon pursued beyond Jordan and slew.
webster_full: ZALMUNNA, n. A king of Midian, the companion of Zebah.
The two escaped from the slaughter at the hill of Moreh with fifteen thousand men.
Gideon pursued them beyond Jordan and took them both at Karkor.
They had slain the brethren of Gideon at mount Tabor.
He slew them, and took away the ornaments that were on their camels' necks.
scriptures: Jdg 8:5
And he said unto the men of Succoth, Give, I pray you, loaves of bread unto the people that follow me; for they be faint, and I am pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna, kings of Midian.
Jdg 8:15

And he came unto the men of Succoth, and said, Behold Zebah and Zalmunna, with whom ye did upbraid me, saying, Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in thine hand, that we should give bread unto thy men that are weary?
Jdg 8:21

Then Zebah and Zalmunna said, Rise thou, and fall upon us: for as the man is, so is his strength. And Gideon arose, and slew Zebah and Zalmunna, and took away the ornaments that were on their camels' necks.
Make their nobles like Oreb, and like Zeeb: yea, all their princes as Zebah, and as Zalmunna:
corruption_summary: Asaph's prayer that God's enemies be made as Zebah and Zalmunna is dismissed as sub-Christian vindictiveness, when the psalm asks judgment for a stated end — that men may seek the LORD's name.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 83 is one of the psalms modern readers are taught to be embarrassed by: a prayer that a coalition of nations be made as Zebah and Zalmunna, as stubble before the wind. The embarrassment misreads the psalm by stopping two verses early. Asaph states his purpose plainly — fill their faces with shame, “that they may seek thy name, O LORD”, and “that men may know that thou, whose name alone is JEHOVAH, art the most high over all the earth” (Psa 83:16, 18). The prayer is that God would break a proud confederacy against His people so thoroughly that its members turn to Him. That is not vindictiveness; it is a plea for judgment as the road to repentance, and it is prayed by a man who has left the vengeance entirely in God's hands.

The second correction is to the idea that such prayers belong to a discarded era. The saints under the altar in Revelation cry “How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?” (Rev 6:10), and they are not rebuked. The New Testament forbids the believer private revenge and commands him to bless his persecutors and feed his enemy; it does not forbid him to long for God to right what is wrong. The dictionary holds both: love of enemies as a present duty, and confidence that the Judge of all the earth shall do right — which is exactly why the Christian need not, and must not, take the sword into his own hand.

“All their princes as Zebah, and as Zalmunna” — a name kept in Israel's prayers.

pos: n. (a Reubenite who joined Korah's rebellion against Moses and was swallowed alive by the earth)
etymology: From Hebrew Dathan, of uncertain derivation. He is never named apart from his brother Abiram; the two are the Reubenite half of a rebellion whose other half was Levitical.
biblical_def: Dathan son of Eliab was a Reubenite, and with his brother Abiram he joined the conspiracy of Korah the Levite against Moses and Aaron (Num 16:1). The alliance is instructive: Korah wanted the priesthood, the Reubenites wanted the civil leadership, and the two grievances found each other. Summoned to answer, they refused with contempt: “And Moses sent to call Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab: which said, We will not come up” (Num 16:12), and they went on to accuse Moses of dragging Israel out of a land flowing with milk and honey — meaning Egypt — to kill them in the wilderness. Judgment came on their own doorsteps. “Dathan and Abiram came out, and stood in the door of their tents, and their wives, and their sons, and their little children” (Num 16:27), and the earth opened her mouth and swallowed them and their households. Numbers records the whole thing again in the second census as a warning to a new generation: “This is that Dathan and Abiram, which were famous in the congregation, who strove against Moses and against Aaron in the company of Korah, when they strove against the LORD” (Num 26:9). That last clause is the doctrine of the passage. To strive against God's appointed servants was, in the end, to strive against the LORD.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Dathan; in sacred history he is a Reubenite who conspired with Korah against Moses, and was swallowed up by the earth.
webster_full: DATHAN, n. The son of Eliab, of the tribe of Reuben.
With his brother Abiram he joined Korah the Levite in rebellion against Moses and Aaron.
Being summoned, he refused to come up, and reproached Moses concerning the land of Egypt.
The earth opened her mouth and swallowed him, with his household and his goods.
Moses recites the judgment in Deuteronomy as a warning to Israel.

Num 26:9

And the sons of Eliab; Nemuel, and Dathan, and Abiram. This is that Dathan and Abiram, which were famous in the congregation, who strove against Moses and against Aaron in the company of Korah, when they strove against the LORD:
corruption_summary: The rebellion is recast as a democratic protest against clerical privilege, and the judgment as an authoritarian atrocity — a reading that has to ignore what the rebels actually said and whom Numbers says they were striving against.
corruption_paragraphs: Korah's slogan sounds admirable in translation: all the congregation are holy, every one of them, wherefore then lift ye up yourselves above the congregation of the LORD? Modern readings take it at face value and make Moses the villain of an egalitarian parable. Two things are fatal to that reading. First, Moses did not lift himself up; God called him from a bush he ran away from, and Numbers calls him the meekest man on the face of the earth. Second, Numbers itself supplies the interpretation: they “strove against the LORD”. Where God has appointed an office, contempt for the office is contempt for the One who gave it. Jude places this episode among his three examples of apostasy — “perished in the gainsaying of Core” (Jud 1:11).

The second corruption is the flinching at the judgment, particularly at the little children standing in the tent doors. The dictionary does not soften it and does not pretend the passage is comfortable. It observes what Scripture observes: that God is the Judge of all the earth and shall do right (Gen 18:25); that households in the ancient covenant order stood or fell with their heads, which is a solemn argument for the weight of a father's choices rather than an argument against God; and that the sons of Korah did not die (Num 26:11), and afterward wrote psalms. Mercy ran even through that ground. Judgment fell where it was earned, and a line was spared where God chose to spare it.

“Stood in the door of their tents” — defiance to the last hour.

pos: n. (brother of Dathan and fellow Reubenite in Korah's rebellion; also the firstborn of Hiel, lost in the rebuilding of Jericho)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Abiram, “my father is exalted”, from 'ab, father, and rum, to be high. The name is a boast about a father, borne by a man who despised the father of his nation.
biblical_def: Abiram son of Eliab stands with his brother Dathan at the head of the Reubenite half of Korah's rebellion (Num 16:1). Their charge against Moses was that he had brought them out of a land flowing with milk and honey to kill them in the wilderness, and that he made himself altogether a prince over them — the accusation of tyranny brought against the meekest man on earth. The end came at their own tent doors, and Moses set it before the next generation as a thing they should never forget: “what he did unto Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab, the son of Reuben: how the earth opened her mouth, and swallowed them up, and their households, and their tents, and all the substance that was in their possession, in the midst of all Israel” (Deu 11:6). The psalmist keeps the memory too: “The earth opened and swallowed up Dathan, and covered the company of Abiram” (Psa 106:17). A second man of the name appears in the reign of Ahab, and his fate is a different kind of warning: Hiel the Bethelite rebuilt Jericho under Joshua's ancient curse, “and laid the foundation thereof in Abiram his firstborn” (1Ki 16:34), five hundred years after the curse was pronounced. God's word does not lapse for age.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Abiram; in sacred history the name belongs to a Reubenite swallowed up with Korah, and to the firstborn of Hiel who rebuilt Jericho.
webster_full: ABIRAM, n. The name signifies my father is exalted.
The son of Eliab, a Reubenite, who with Dathan his brother joined the conspiracy of Korah.
He would not come up when Moses sent for him, and perished when the earth opened.
Moses recounts the judgment in Deuteronomy, that Israel might fear.
The firstborn of Hiel the Bethelite bore the same name, and died when his father laid the foundation of Jericho.

And Moses sent to call Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab: which said, We will not come up:
Deu 11:6

And what he did unto Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab, the son of Reuben: how the earth opened her mouth, and swallowed them up, and their households, and their tents, and all the substance that was in their possession, in the midst of all Israel:
The earth opened and swallowed up Dathan, and covered the company of Abiram.
corruption_summary: The claim that Egypt was “a land flowing with milk and honey” is the classic nostalgia of the discontented heart, and it is still the standard argument of every soul that looks back from a hard obedience.
corruption_paragraphs: The most revealing sentence Dathan and Abiram ever spoke was their description of Egypt. The phrase “a land that floweth with milk and honey” belongs to Canaan throughout the Pentateuch; they took the promise's own words and pinned them on the house of bondage. That is what discontent does to memory. Men who had groaned under taskmasters and cried to God out of the brick-kilns now remembered Egypt as plenty and called the wilderness a murder plot. Paul catalogues the wilderness sins as written warnings for the church — “Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured, and were destroyed of the destroyer” (1Co 10:10) — and murmuring is treated there as a lethal sin, not a mood.

The second Abiram carries a warning of a different sort, and it is worth naming because the modern mind assumes that old words expire. Joshua cursed the man who should rebuild Jericho, and five centuries later, in the reign of Ahab, Hiel did it and lost his firstborn laying the foundation and his youngest setting up the gates — “according to the word of the LORD, which he spake by Joshua the son of Nun” (1Ki 16:34). Nothing had faded. This is the doctrine of Scripture concerning its own words: “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8), and the Lord Jesus put it beyond argument — one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law till all be fulfilled.

“Laid the foundation thereof in Abiram his firstborn” — a curse five hundred years old, still standing.
A name meaning “my father is exalted”, borne by a man who despised authority.

pos: n. (son of Ebed; the demagogue who talked Shechem into revolt against Abimelech and fled at the first sight of his army)
etymology: From Hebrew Ga'al, connected with a root meaning to loathe or cast off — not the homonym ga'al, to redeem. He is always “Gaal the son of Ebed”, and Ebed means servant.
biblical_def: Gaal the son of Ebed appears for sixteen verses in Judges 9 and does more damage in them than most men manage in a lifetime. Abimelech, having murdered seventy of his brothers to make himself king, had ruled Shechem three years when God sent an evil spirit between him and the men of the city. Into that opening walked Gaal: “Gaal the son of Ebed came with his brethren, and went over to Shechem: and the men of Shechem put their confidence in him” (Jdg 9:26). He waited for the vintage feast, and when the wine was in he made his speech: “Who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him? is not he the son of Jerubbaal?… serve the men of Hamor the father of Shechem: for why should we serve him?” (Jdg 9:28). It is pure demagoguery — an appeal to older blood, a sneer at the ruler's parentage, a promise to lead if only the people would give him the army. Zebul, the city's officer, sent word to Abimelech; and when the attack came at dawn Gaal stood on the gate and could not tell soldiers from shadows (Jdg 9:36). He was beaten, and “Zebul thrust out Gaal and his brethren, that they should not dwell in Shechem” (Jdg 9:41). The city he stirred up was destroyed; the man who stirred it was merely evicted.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Gaal; in sacred history he is the son of Ebed, who raised Shechem in revolt against Abimelech and was driven out.
webster_full: GAAL, n. The son of Ebed, a stranger who came to dwell in Shechem.
The men of Shechem put their confidence in him, in the third year of Abimelech.
At the feast of their vintage he spoke against Abimelech, and offered to lead them.
Zebul, the officer of the city, sent privily to Abimelech and betrayed the plot.
Gaal was defeated in the gate, and thrust out of Shechem with his brethren.
scriptures: Jdg 9:26
And Gaal the son of Ebed came with his brethren, and went over to Shechem: and the men of Shechem put their confidence in him.
Jdg 9:28

And Gaal the son of Ebed said, Who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him? is not he the son of Jerubbaal? and Zebul his officer? serve the men of Hamor the father of Shechem: for why should we serve him?
Jdg 9:36
And when Gaal saw the people, he said to Zebul, Behold, there come people down from the top of the mountains. And Zebul said unto him, Thou seest the shadow of the mountains as if they were men.
Jdg 9:41
And Abimelech dwelt at Arumah: and Zebul thrust out Gaal and his brethren, that they should not dwell in Shechem.
corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is discernment about the men a people trusts — and that a rebellion against a wicked ruler is not thereby a righteous cause.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Gaal is too obscure to have attracted a controversy. What his brief career supplies is a portrait the church needs and rarely draws: the opportunist who arrives in a season of discontent, says what the aggrieved want said, offers himself as the remedy, and cannot deliver anything at all. The men of Shechem “put their confidence in him” on no evidence whatever — a stranger, newly arrived, loud at a feast. Scripture is full of warnings against exactly this credulity: “The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going” (Pro 14:15), and the Lord Jesus warned of those who come in their own name, whom men receive (Joh 5:43).

The principle to recover is that opposition to a wicked man is not by itself a righteous cause. Abimelech was a fratricide and a tyrant, and Judges says God Himself sent the spirit of discord that undid him — but Gaal was no deliverer, only a rival with a better speech. Judges 9 ends with both parties destroyed and the writer explaining that God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech and the wickedness of the men of Shechem upon their own heads (Jdg 9:56-57). The believer is not required to choose between two evils, and is required to weigh a leader by his character and his fidelity to God rather than by the sharpness of his complaint. “Ye shall know them by their fruits” (Mat 7:16).

“Who is Abimelech… that we should serve him?” — the demagogue's question, then and since.
“Thou seest the shadow of the mountains as if they were men” — the mockery of a man out of his depth.

pos: n. (a captain of Ishbosheth who murdered his master in bed and brought the head to David expecting reward)
etymology: From Hebrew Ba'anah, commonly explained as “in affliction” or “son of affliction”. The name is borne by several men in Scripture; this one is remembered for one act.
biblical_def: Baanah and his brother Rechab were Benjamites of Beeroth, captains of raiding bands under Ishbosheth, Saul's surviving son (2Sa 4:2). With Abner dead and the house of Saul collapsing, the two calculated where the future lay. They came into the house at noon, “as though they would have fetched wheat; and they smote him under the fifth rib: and Rechab and Baanah his brother escaped” (2Sa 4:6), carried the head of Ishbosheth all night through the plain to Hebron, and laid it before David with a speech about the LORD avenging the king upon Saul and his seed. They had entirely misjudged the man. David had already executed the Amalekite who claimed to have finished Saul, and his answer here is colder still: “As the LORD liveth, who hath redeemed my soul out of all adversity” (2Sa 4:9) — then a reminder of what he had done to the last man who brought him such news, and the sentence: “How much more, when wicked men have slain a righteous person in his own house upon his bed?” He commanded his young men, and they slew them, and cut off their hands and their feet, and hanged them up over the pool in Hebron (2Sa 4:12). Ishbosheth's head was buried honourably in Abner's tomb. David would take the kingdom from God's hand or not at all.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Baanah; in sacred history he is a captain of Ishbosheth who with his brother murdered his master, and was put to death by David.
webster_full: BAANAH, n. A son of Rimmon the Beerothite, of the children of Benjamin.
He and his brother Rechab were captains of bands under Ishbosheth the son of Saul.
They slew their master upon his bed at noon, and carried his head to David at Hebron.
David caused them to be slain, and their hands and feet cut off, and their bodies hanged over the pool.
The name is borne also by others in the books of Samuel, Ezra and Nehemiah.
scriptures: And Saul's son had two men that were captains of bands: the name of the one was Baanah, and the name of the other Rechab, the sons of Rimmon a Beerothite, of the children of Benjamin: (for Beeroth also was reckoned to Benjamin:
And they came thither into the midst of the house, as though they would have fetched wheat; and they smote him under the fifth rib: and Rechab and Baanah his brother escaped.
And David answered Rechab and Baanah his brother, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, and said unto them, As the LORD liveth, who hath redeemed my soul out of all adversity,

And David commanded his young men, and they slew them, and cut off their hands and their feet, and hanged them up over the pool in Hebron. But they took the head of Ishbosheth, and buried it in the sepulchre of Abner in Hebron.
corruption_summary: The murderers invoked the LORD's vengeance to sanctify their own ambition — the perennial corruption of putting God's name over a sin already decided on.
corruption_paragraphs: The most striking thing about Baanah and Rechab is not the murder but the theology they brought with it. They laid a severed head before David and said the LORD had avenged the king that day of Saul and of his seed. They had a doctrine of providence and they used it to bless a knife. This is a permanent temptation and not an ancient one: to identify one's own advantage with the will of God, to read a providence as a permission, and to speak piously over a thing conscience already condemned. Scripture's judgment on the method is severe: “Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil” (Isa 5:20). David did not argue theology with them. He named the act — wicked men slaying a righteous person in his own house upon his bed — and executed the sentence.

The second thing to draw out is David's consistency, because it is the reason he is worth imitating here. He had refused twice to lift his hand against Saul when the chance was in front of him. He had executed the Amalekite who claimed the credit for Saul's death. He mourned Abner publicly so that all Israel knew it was not his doing. And now he refuses a throne handed to him on a plate. He would receive the kingdom from God or not receive it, and every shortcut offered him he cut down. That is the same temptation the second David refused in the wilderness, when all the kingdoms of the world were offered on one condition — and the answer was, “Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve” (Mat 4:10).

A crown offered by treachery, and refused.

pos: n. pl. (a sea-coast people of the Philistine country, and the name of David's foreign bodyguard under Benaiah)
etymology: From Hebrew Kerethi, associated with the sea-coast and commonly connected with Crete. Ezekiel spells the plural Cherethims. Always paired in David's service with the Pelethites.
biblical_def: Cherethites is used two ways in Scripture and both matter. Geographically they are a people of the Philistine sea-coast — the Amalekite raiders tell David, “We made an invasion upon the south of the Cherethites, and upon the coast which belongeth to Judah” (1Sa 30:14) — and the prophets name them under judgment with the Philistines: “I will cut off the Cherethims, and destroy the remnant of the sea coast” (Eze 25:16), and “Woe unto the inhabitants of the sea coast, the nation of the Cherethites!” (Zep 2:5). Militarily they are David's household guard. “Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over both the Cherethites and the Pelethites” (2Sa 8:18), and they appear at every crisis of the reign: they go out with him when he flees Absalom — “all the Cherethites, and all the Pelethites, and all the Gittites, six hundred men which came after him from Gath, passed on before the king” (2Sa 15:18) — and they stand with Zadok and Nathan at Solomon's anointing while Adonijah's party is feasting. The point is not incidental. The men who never left David were foreigners, gathered in his outlaw years, loyal when Israel's own tribes and his own son were not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for the Cherethites; in sacred history they are a people of the Philistine sea coast, and the name of David's life guard.
webster_full: CHERETHITES, n. plu. A people dwelling on the sea coast in the south of the land of the Philistines.
They are named with the Philistines in the prophecies of Ezekiel and Zephaniah.
The name is also given to the guard of David, joined always with the Pelethites.
Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was set over both.
They attended the king in his flight from Absalom, and at the anointing of Solomon.
scriptures: We made an invasion upon the south of the Cherethites, and upon the coast which belongeth to Judah, and upon the south of Caleb; and we burned Ziklag with fire.
And all his servants passed on beside him; and all the Cherethites, and all the Pelethites, and all the Gittites, six hundred men which came after him from Gath, passed on before the king.
Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I will stretch out mine hand upon the Philistines, and I will cut off the Cherethims, and destroy the remnant of the sea coast.
Zep 2:5

Woe unto the inhabitants of the sea coast, the nation of the Cherethites! the word of the LORD is against you; O Canaan, the land of the Philistines, I will even destroy thee, that there shall be no inhabitant.
corruption_summary: There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that God has always gathered outsiders into the service of His anointed, and that covenant loyalty is not a matter of birth.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Cherethites are a footnote in military history and have attracted no controversy. What they quietly overturn is an assumption that runs deep in every religious community — that faithfulness tracks pedigree. David's most reliable men were Gentiles: Cherethites and Pelethites from the coast, six hundred Gittites out of Gath, and Ittai the Gittite, who had arrived the day before and answered the king's offer of release with a vow that would not be improved on: “in what place my lord the king shall be, whether in death or life, even there also will thy servant be” (2Sa 15:21). Uriah the Hittite belongs to the same company, and shames the king in the same way.

The principle to recover is that the covenant has always had room for the stranger who takes hold of it, and that the New Testament does not invent this but completes it. Rahab and Ruth are in the genealogy; Isaiah promised the son of the stranger who joins himself to the LORD that he would not be separated from His people (Isa 56:3); and Paul brings it home to every Gentile believer: “Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God” (Eph 2:19). A man's birth does not qualify him and does not disqualify him. What tells is whether he stays with the king when the king is going out over the brook Kidron with his head covered.

pos: n. (the national god of Moab, called by Scripture the abomination of Moab; a high place was built for him by Solomon and defiled by Josiah)
etymology: From Hebrew Kemosh, of uncertain derivation, possibly connected with a root meaning to subdue. Moab is called “the people of Chemosh”, the nation being identified with the idol it served.
biblical_def: Chemosh is the god of Moab, and Scripture treats him with a mixture of contempt and deadly seriousness. Contempt, because he cannot save his own: “Woe to thee, Moab! thou art undone, O people of Chemosh: he hath given his sons that escaped, and his daughters, into captivity unto Sihon king of the Amorites” (Num 21:29). Seriousness, because his worship was the ruin of Israel's wisest king. “Then did Solomon build an high place for Chemosh, the abomination of Moab, in the hill that is before Jerusalem” (1Ki 11:7) — built by the man who had built the temple, on the hill facing it, for the wives who turned away his heart. The LORD named the offence when He tore the kingdom in two: “because that they have forsaken me, and have worshipped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, Chemosh the god of the Moabites, and Milcom the god of the children of Ammon” (1Ki 11:33). Three hundred years later Josiah went out and defiled those same high places, still standing on what Kings calls the mount of corruption (2Ki 23:13). Jephthah, negotiating with Ammon, speaks of Chemosh as the god the enemy believes gives him land (Jdg 11:24) — the diplomat's courtesy, not a concession; Jephthah's own confidence is in the LORD who is Judge.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Chemosh; in sacred history he is the national idol of the Moabites, called the abomination of Moab.
webster_full: CHEMOSH, n. The chief idol of the Moabites, and reckoned also among the gods of Ammon.
Moab is called in the book of Numbers the people of Chemosh.
Solomon built an high place for Chemosh on the hill before Jerusalem, for his strange wives.
For this and the like idolatries the kingdom was rent from his son.
Josiah defiled the high places which Solomon had builded, on the mount of corruption.
scriptures: Woe to thee, Moab! thou art undone, O people of Chemosh: he hath given his sons that escaped, and his daughters, into captivity unto Sihon king of the Amorites.
Then did Solomon build an high place for Chemosh, the abomination of Moab, in the hill that is before Jerusalem, and for Molech, the abomination of the children of Ammon.

Because that they have forsaken me, and have worshipped Ashtoreth the goddess of the Zidonians, Chemosh the god of the Moabites, and Milcom the god of the children of Ammon, and have not walked in my ways, to do that which is right in mine eyes, and to keep my statutes and my judgments, as did David his father.
Wilt not thou possess that which Chemosh thy god giveth thee to possess? So whomsoever the LORD our God shall drive out from before us, them will we possess.
corruption_summary: Israel's religion is described as one national cult among several — the LORD for Israel, Chemosh for Moab — when the Old Testament's whole claim is that the idols are nothing and the LORD alone is God.
corruption_paragraphs: A standard academic reading treats early Israel as henotheistic: each nation had its god, Chemosh belonged to Moab as the LORD belonged to Israel, and strict monotheism developed later. Jephthah's sentence about “Chemosh thy god” is the usual proof-text. It will not carry the weight. Jephthah is arguing with a pagan king in the king's own terms, as Paul quoted the Athenian poets without endorsing them, and he closes by appealing to “the LORD the Judge” over both nations. The Pentateuch itself, long before, is explicit: “the LORD he is God in heaven above, and upon the earth beneath: there is none else” (Deu 4:39). The idols are not rival deities; they are, as the psalmist says, the work of men's hands, and behind them, as Paul says, are devils and not God (1Co 10:20).

The second corruption is a failure to feel the horror of Solomon's high place. The wisest man who ever lived, who had seen the glory fill the house he built, put a shrine to the abomination of Moab on the facing hill because his wives wanted it. Kings does not say he stopped believing; it says “his wives turned away his heart” (1Ki 11:3). Syncretism rarely announces itself as apostasy. It arrives as accommodation, as peace in the household, as tolerance for what someone loved brought with them — and three centuries later a reforming king is still tearing out what one man permitted. “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (1Jn 5:21) is the last sentence of John's epistle, written to Christians, not Moabites.
